title: CJI Surya Kant Defends NALSAR Students' Right to Protest After BCI Enrolment Ban
excerpt: India's Chief Justice stayed the Bar Council's punitive action against law graduates who opposed his convocation invitation, affirming their constitutional right to peaceful dissent.
body:
• Chief Justice of India Surya Kant criticized the Bar Council of India for barring NALSAR's 2026 law graduates from enrolling as advocates after they opposed his convocation invitation.
  • Over 450 NALSAR students signed a petition citing the CJI's handling of a plea concerning police action against Jantar Mantar protesters on July 20.
  • BCI Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra retaliated by halting graduate enrolments, but withdrew the circular after widespread backlash.
  • The Supreme Court stayed all coercive action and the CJI welcomed NALSAR graduates to join the Supreme Court Bar for legal aid work.

In an extraordinary sequence of events, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant has personally rebuked the Bar Council of India (BCI) for retaliating against law students who opposed his invitation as their convocation chief guest—and affirmed their fundamental right to protest, even against the country's highest judicial authority.

The controversy began when more than 450 students at the National Academy of Legal Studies and Research (NALSAR), Hyderabad, signed a petition urging the university to reconsider its reported plan to invite CJI Surya Kant as chief guest for its 2026 convocation ceremony.

The Students' Objection

The students' primary concern centered on the Supreme Court's handling of a plea about alleged police action against protesters during the "Chalo Sansad" (March to Parliament) demonstration at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on July 20, 2026. The protest, organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), raised issues including the conduct of the NEET examination and reforms in the National Testing Agency.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2088945802584653832

According to student representations, when the matter was mentioned for urgent hearing on July 22, the CJI told counsel, "Don't waste our time, and don't waste your time." When counsel offered to show video evidence of alleged police excesses, the CJI reportedly responded, "We are not interested in videos; we don't have time to watch."

The students said that receiving their degrees from a dignitary "whose recent public conduct, as reported, appears dismissive of serious allegations of police brutality against protesting citizens, sits uncomfortably with what we have been taught to value during our time at NALSAR." A separate petition before the CJI cited injuries to more than 170 protesters, including women and children.

"A convocation is meant to be a moment where the University's own values, including a commitment to constitutional rights, access to justice, and reasoned engagement with grievances, are visibly reflected in the choices it makes."

— NALSAR Student Representation, July 2026

BCI's Punitive Response

The situation escalated sharply when BCI Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra issued a circular directing all State Bar Councils not to enrol NALSAR's 2026 law graduates as advocates, pending an inquiry into the students' campaign. The BCI asserted that students showing disrespect toward the country's highest judicial office could not become responsible advocates and alleged political instigation by certain faculty members.

The move drew widespread public backlash. Legal observers pointed out that no formal BCI Council meeting had been convened to authorize the Chairman's unilateral action. Under pressure, the BCI modified its position, withdrew the enrolment ban, and eventually closed all proceedings against the students.

CJI's Remarkable Response

When a writ petition challenging the BCI's directives came before the Supreme Court, CJI Surya Kant—the very target of the students' protest—took an approach that surprised many observers. Sitting on a bench with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, the Chief Justice strongly criticized the BCI's intervention.

He emphasized that the dispute, "if any, was a direct dialogue between himself and the students," and questioned why the BCI had chosen to intervene at all. Recalling his own involvement in student leadership activities during his youth, the CJI affirmed that students possess a fundamental right to protest peacefully, even when their position may be mistaken.

Justice Bagchi pointedly asked whether any formal resolution had been passed to authorize the BCI circular. The Court issued notice to the BCI, directing a counter-affidavit within two weeks, and stayed all coercive action against students and faculty.

An Unexpected Gesture

In a striking conclusion to the hearing, CJI Surya Kant welcomed the NALSAR graduates to enrol without delay and join the Supreme Court Bar. He announced the Court would empanel them for legal aid cases, describing it as "a befitting answer to those who had attempted to create impediments in their legal careers."

NALSAR has not announced a convocation date or confirmed the chief guest. CJI Surya Kant has previously disputed media reports about the July 20 proceedings, clarifying on July 24 that no writ petition seeking urgent intervention had been filed—only a representation had reached him.

What It Signals

The episode has become a defining moment in the ongoing conversation about judicial accountability and student activism in India. The CJI's decision to uphold the students' right to dissent—even when the dissent was directed at him—has drawn praise from legal scholars as a powerful affirmation of constitutional values. For the many Indian diaspora families with children pursuing legal education in India, it underscores both the vitality and the tensions within India's legal institutions.
